claim: Proinflammatory extracellular chromatin from neutrophil extracellular traps (NETs) and other cellular sources is found in COVID-19 patients.
source: Prinflammatory extracellular chromatin from neutrophil extracellular traps (NETs) and other cellular sources is found in COVID-19 patients and may promote pathology.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as background information without specific data from this study, suggesting it is based on prior knowledge or literature.

claim: Extracellular chromatin from NETs and other cellular sources may promote pathology in COVID-19 patients.
source: Prinflammatory extracellular chromatin from neutrophil extracellular traps (NETs) and other cellular sources is found in COVID-19 patients and may promote pathology.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the potential role of extracellular chromatin in disease pathology.

claim: Dornase alfa reduced C-reactive protein (CRP) by 33% compared to the combined BAC groups.
source: Dornase alfa was well tolerated and reduced CRP by 33% compared to the combined BAC groups (T-BAC).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the trial data presented in the abstract.

claim: Least squares mean post-dexamethasone CRP fell from 101.9 mg/L to 23.23 mg/L in R-BAC +DA participants at 7 days.
source: Least squares (LS) mean post-dexamethasone CRP fell from 101.9 mg/L to 23.23 mg/L in R-BAC +DA participants versus a 99.5 mg/L to 34.82 mg/L reduction in the T-BAC group at 7 days; p=0.01.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the primary endpoint analysis.

claim: Least squares mean post-dexamethasone CRP fell from 99.5 mg/L to 34.82 mg/L in the T-BAC group at 7 days.
source: Least squares (LS) mean post-dexamethasone CRP fell from 101.9 mg/L to 23.23 mg/L in R-BAC +DA participants versus a 99.5 mg/L to 34.82 mg/L reduction in the T-BAC group at 7 days; p=0.01.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the primary endpoint analysis for the control group.

claim: The difference in CRP reduction between R-BAC +DA and T-BAC groups was statistically significant (p=0.01).
source: Least squares (LS) mean post-dexamethasone CRP fell from 101.9 mg/L to 23.23 mg/L in R-BAC +DA participants versus a 99.5 mg/L to 34.82 mg/L reduction in the T-BAC group at 7 days; p=0.01.
evidence: This is a statistical result from the primary endpoint analysis.

claim: Dornase alfa increased live discharge rates by 63% (HR 1.63, 95% CI 1.01–2.61, p=0.03).
source: Dornase alfa increased live discharge rates by 63% (HR 1.63, 95% CI 1.01–2.61, p=0.03)
evidence: This is a secondary outcome result from the trial data.

claim: Dornase alfa increased lymphocyte counts (LS mean: 1.08 vs 0.87, p=0.02).
source: Dornase alfa increased live discharge rates by 63% (HR 1.63, 95% CI 1.01–2.61, p=0.03), increased lymphocyte counts (LS mean: 1.08 vs 0.87, p=0.02)
evidence: This is a secondary outcome result from the trial data.

claim: Dornase alfa reduced circulating cf-DNA.
source: Dornase alfa increased live discharge rates by 63% (HR 1.63, 95% CI 1.01–2.61, p=0.03), increased lymphocyte counts (LS mean: 1.08 vs 0.87, p=0.02) and reduced circulating cf-DNA and the coagulopathy marker D-dimer (LS mean: 570.78 vs 1656.96 μg/mL, p=0.004).
evidence: This is a secondary outcome result from the trial data.

claim: Dornase alfa reduced the coagulopathy marker D-dimer (LS mean: 570.78 vs 1656.96 μg/mL, p=0.004).
source: Dornase alfa increased live discharge rates by 63% (HR 1.63, 95% CI 1.01–2.61, p=0.03), increased lymphocyte counts (LS mean: 1.08 vs 0.87, p=0.02) and reduced circulating cf-DNA and the coagulopathy marker D-dimer (LS mean: 570.78 vs 1656.96 μg/mL, p=0.004).
evidence: This is a secondary outcome result from the trial data.

claim: SARS-CoV-2 pneumonia can lead to hyperinflammation, coagulopathy, respiratory failure, and death.
source: SARS-CoV-2 pneumonia can lead to hyperinflammation, coagulopathy, respiratory failure, and death (Siddiqi and Mehra, 2020; Zhou et al., 2020), even with less pathogenic variants and in immunized patients (American Thoracic Society, 2000).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: SARS-CoV-2 pneumonia can lead to severe outcomes even with less pathogenic variants and in immunized patients.
source: SARS-CoV-2 pneumonia can lead to hyperinflammation, coagulopathy, respiratory failure, and death (Siddiqi and Mehra, 2020; Zhou et al., 2020), even with less pathogenic variants and in immunized patients (American Thoracic Society, 2000).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation.

claim: In severe COVID-19 pneumonia, neutrophil activation drives neutrophil extracellular trap (NET) formation.
source: In severe COVID-19 pneumonia, neutrophil activation drives neutrophil extracellular trap (NET) formation (Radermecker et al., 2020; Zuo et al., 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: NETs are composed of DNA-histone complexes that are associated with coagulopathy and endothelial dysfunction.
source: NETs, are composed of DNA-histone complexes that are associated with coagulopathy and endothelial dysfunction (Papayannopoulos, 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Extracellular histones from NETs or other cellular sources promote inflammation, immune dysfunction, and lethality in sepsis.
source: Extracellular histones from NETs, or other cellular sources such as dying lymphocytes, promote inflammation, immune dysfunction, and lethality in sepsis (Ioannou et al., 2022; Tsourouktsoglou et al., 2020; Xu et al., 2011; Xu et al., 2009).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Digestion of chromatin DNA by endonucleases suppresses the proinflammatory activity of histones and enables their clearance from the circulation.
source: Digestion of chromatin DNA by endonucleases suppresses the proinflammatory activity of histones and enables their clearance from the circulation (Ioannou et al., 2022; Tsourouktsoglou et al., 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: DNAse I treatment reduces pathology in murine pulmonary viral infections.
source: Consistently, DNAse I treatment reduces pathology in murine pulmonary viral infections (Cortjens et al., 2018; Pillai et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Endogenous DNAse activity and NET clearance capacity are defective in severe COVID-19 pneumonia.
source: Endogenous DNAse activity and NET clearance capacity are defective in severe COVID-19 pneumonia, and the extent of these defects correlates with mortality (Aramburu et al., 2022).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: The extent of defects in endogenous DNAse activity and NET clearance capacity correlates with mortality in severe COVID-19 pneumonia.
source: Endogenous DNAse activity and NET clearance capacity are defective in severe COVID-19 pneumonia, and the extent of these defects correlates with mortality (Aramburu et al., 2022).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Dornase alfa is a recombinant human DNase approved since 1993 for patients with cystic fibrosis (CF).
source: Dornase alfa, the active ingredient in pulmozyme, is a recombinant human DNase approved since 1993 for patients with cystic fibrosis (CF) (Konstan and Ratjen, 2012; Lazarus and Wagener, 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Dornase alfa solubilizes NETs, reduces inflammation, and improves pulmonary function in chronic and acute exacerbations of CF.
source: Dornase alfa solubilizes NETs, reduces inflammation, and improves pulmonary function in chronic and acute exacerbations of CF (Konstan and Ratjen, 2012; Papayannopoulos et al., 2011).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Pulmozyme is safe and well-tolerated in children and adults with CF at doses up to 10 mg taken twice daily.
source: Pulmozyme is safe and well-tolerated in children and adults with CF at doses up to 10 mg taken twice daily.
evidence: This statement is presented as established knowledge about the drug.

claim: Nebulized pulmozyme administration does not increase circulating endonucleases.
source: Since nebulized pulmozyme administration does not increase circulating endonucleases, it remains unclear whether the degradation of extracellular chromatin in the lungs would reduce circulating chromatin and systemic hyper-inflammation in viral infections.
evidence: This is stated as a known fact that leads to uncertainty about systemic effects.

claim: CRP is a reliable marker of systemic inflammation in severe infection.
source: CRP is a reliable marker of systemic inflammation in severe infection (McArdle et al., 2004).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: In patients infected with COVID-19, a high CRP of ≥40 mg/L carried a poor prognosis.
source: In patients infected with COVID-19, a high CRP of ≥40 mg/L carried a poor prognosis with a lower cut-off of ≥35 mg/L in the elderly (Villoteau et al., 2021), particularly when combined with lymphopenia and coagulopathy marked by elevated D-dimer (Fisher et al., 2022; Liu et al., 2020; Luo et al., 2020; Smilowitz et al., 2021; Tornling et al., 2021; Ullah et al., 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Poor outcomes in COVID-19 are associated with an early rise in CRP.
source: Poor outcomes are associated with an early rise (Mueller et al., 2020), higher peak, and delayed reduction in CRP (Cui et al., 2021).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Poor outcomes in COVID-19 are associated with a higher peak CRP.
source: Poor outcomes are associated with an early rise (Mueller et al., 2020), higher peak, and delayed reduction in CRP (Cui et al., 2021).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Poor outcomes in COVID-19 are associated with delayed reduction in CRP.
source: Poor outcomes are associated with an early rise (Mueller et al., 2020), higher peak, and delayed reduction in CRP (Cui et al., 2021).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Elevated IL-6 and CRP can predict the need for mechanical ventilation in COVID-19.
source: Moreover, elevated IL-6 and CRP can predict the need for mechanical ventilation (Herold et al., 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: CRP correlated well with levels of DNA and NET degradation activity in COVID-19 patient plasma.
source: In addition, CRP correlated well with levels of DNA and NET degradation activity in COVID-19 patient plasma suggesting a link between CRP and the capacity to degrade cell free (cf)-DNA in the circulation (Aramburu et al., 2022).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: CRP became a reliable primary endpoint in subsequent trials that demonstrated the effectiveness of other systemic therapies such as namilumab or infliximab that target inflammatory cytokines.
source: CRP became a reliable primary endpoint in subsequent trials that demonstrated the effectiveness of other systemic therapies such as namilumab or infliximab that target inflammatory cytokines (Fisher et al., 2022).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: The COVASE trial was initiated in June 2020 and was completed in October 2021.
source: The trial was initiated in June 2020 and was completed in October 2021.
evidence: This is a factual statement about the trial timeline.

claim: At the start of the COVASE trial, only dexamethasone had been proven to benefit hospitalized COVID-19 pneumonia patients.
source: At the start of the trial, only dexamethasone had been proven to benefit hospitalized COVID-19 pneumonia patients and was thus included in both arms of the trial.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of knowledge at the time the trial began.

claim: Dexamethasone was included in both arms of the COVASE trial.
source: At the start of the trial, only dexamethasone had been proven to benefit hospitalized COVID-19 pneumonia patients and was thus included in both arms of the trial.
evidence: This is a statement about the trial design.

claim: The COVASE trial recruited 39 evaluable participants: 30 randomized to dornase alfa (R-BAC +DA), 9 randomized to BAC (R-BAC), and included 60 CC-BAC participants.
source: We recruited 39 evaluable participants: 30 randomized to dornase alfa (R-BAC +DA), 9 randomized to BAC (R-BAC), and included 60 CC-BAC participants.
evidence: This is a factual statement about the trial enrollment.

claim: Dornase alfa was well tolerated in the COVASE trial.
source: Dornase alfa was well tolerated and reduced CRP by 33% compared to the combined BAC groups (T-BAC).
evidence: This is a finding from the trial regarding safety.

claim: The anti-inflammatory effect of dornase alfa was confirmed with subgroup and sensitivity analyses on randomised participants only.
source: The anti-inflammatory effect of dornase alfa was further confirmed with subgroup and sensitivity analyses on randomised participants only, mitigating potential biases associated with the use of CC-BAC participants.
evidence: This is a statement about the robustness of the findings through additional analyses.

claim: The COVASE trial was sponsored by University College London (UCL) and carried out at UCLH.
source: The trial was sponsored by University College London (UCL) and carried out at UCLH with ethical (REC: 20/SC/0197, Protocol: 132333, RAS ID:283091) and UK MHRA approvals.
evidence: This is a factual statement about the trial administration.

claim: The COVASE trial received ethical approval (REC: 20/SC/0197, Protocol: 132333, RAS ID:283091) and UK MHRA approvals.
source: The trial was sponsored by University College London (UCL) and carried out at UCLH with ethical (REC: 20/SC/0197, Protocol: 132333, RAS ID:283091) and UK MHRA approvals.
evidence: This is a factual statement about regulatory approvals.

claim: All randomized participants in the COVASE trial provided informed consent.
source: All randomized participants provided informed consent.
evidence: This is a statement about ethical procedures in the trial.

claim: The COVASE trial was a single-site, randomized, controlled, parallel, open-label investigation.
source: The COVASE trial was a single-site, randomized, controlled, parallel, open-label investigation.
evidence: This is a statement about the trial design.

claim: The primary endpoint of the COVASE trial was change in CRP.
source: The primary endpoint was change in CRP.
evidence: This is a statement about the trial design.

claim: Eligible COVASE participants were randomly assigned (3:1) to either the BAC plus nebulized dornase alfa (R-BAC +DA) or the R-BAC group alone.
source: Eligible, consented participants were randomly assigned (3:1) to either the BAC plus nebulized dornase alfa (R-BAC +DA) or the R-BAC group alone.
evidence: This is a statement about the trial design and randomization.

claim: Participants randomized to the active arm of the COVASE trial received twice daily 2.5 mg nebulized dornase alfa in addition to BAC from day 1–7.
source: From day 1–7, participants that were randomized to the active arm received twice daily 2.5 mg nebulized dornase alfa in addition to BAC.
evidence: This is a statement about the treatment protocol.

claim: In all cases in the COVASE trial, BAC included dexamethasone (6 mg/day) for 10 days or until discharge, whichever was shorter.
source: In all cases BAC included dexamethasone (6 mg/day) for 10 days or until discharge, whichever was shorter as established in the RECOVERY trial (Horby et al., 2021).
evidence: This is a statement about the treatment protocol with a citation to the RECOVERY trial.

claim: The primary analysis of the COVASE trial was performed on samples up to day 7.
source: The primary analysis was performed on samples up to day 7.
evidence: This is a statement about the analysis plan.

claim: The final trial visit in the COVASE trial occurred on day 35.
source: The final trial visit occurred on day 35.
evidence: This is a statement about the trial protocol.

claim: For every COVASE participant randomized to the active treatment, two matched CC-BAC participants were included.
source: For every COVASE participant randomized to the active treatment, two matched CC-BAC participants were included.
evidence: This is a statement about the trial design.

claim: CC-BAC participants were admitted to UCLH over the same time as randomized patients and treated with the same BAC regimen, including dexamethasone.
source: CC-BAC participants were admitted to UCLH over the same time as randomized patients and treated with the same BAC regimen, including dexamethasone.
evidence: This is a statement about the control group selection.

claim: CC-BAC participants fulfilled the inclusion and exclusion criteria of the COVASE study.
source: CC-BAC participants fulfilled the inclusion and exclusion criteria of the COVASE study and were matched for age, gender, BMI, comorbidities and CRP.
evidence: This is a statement about the control group selection criteria.

claim: CC-BAC participants were matched for age, gender, BMI, comorbidities and CRP.
source: CC-BAC participants fulfilled the inclusion and exclusion criteria of the COVASE study and were matched for age, gender, BMI, comorbidities and CRP.
evidence: This is a statement about the matching criteria for controls.

claim: Eligible COVASE trial participants were male and female, aged ≥18 years, who were hospitalized for suspected SARS-CoV-2 infection confirmed by PCR test.
source: Male and female participants, aged ≥18 years, who were hospitalized for suspected Coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV–2) infection confirmed by polymerase chain reaction (PCR) test and optionally with radiological confirmation with chest CT.
evidence: This is a statement about the inclusion criteria.

claim: Eligible COVASE trial participants had stable oxygen saturation (≥94%) on supplementary oxygen and a CRP ≥30 mg/L.
source: Participants with stable oxygen saturation (≥94%) on supplementary oxygen and a CRP ≥30 mg/L.
evidence: This is a statement about the inclusion criteria.

claim: The primary outcome of the COVASE trial was the least square (LS) mean CRP concentration up to 7 days or at hospital discharge whichever was sooner.
source: The primary outcome was the least square (LS) mean CRP concentration up to 7 days or at hospital discharge whichever was sooner.
evidence: This is a statement about the primary outcome definition.

claim: Pre-specified secondary outcomes of the COVASE trial included days on oxygen, time to hospital discharge, mortality by day 35, and changes in clinically relevant biomarkers including lymphocyte count and D-dimer levels.
source: Pre-specified secondary outcomes included days on oxygen; time to hospital discharge; mortality by day 35; and changes in clinically relevant biomarkers including lymphocyte count and D-dimer levels.
evidence: This is a statement about the secondary outcomes.

claim: From June 2020 to October 2021, 41 participants were recruited and randomized to the COVASE trial.
source: From June 2020 to October 2021, 41 participants were recruited and randomized, with 1 participant in R-BAC group discharged before a second CRP measurement who was excluded from all analyses except for safety (CONSORT Diagram: Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a factual statement about trial enrollment.

claim: 39 participants were included in the ITT analysis set of the COVASE trial: 30 R-BAC +DA and 9 R-BAC.
source: Therefore, 39 participants were included in the ITT analysis set, 30 R-BAC +DA and 9 R-BAC.
evidence: This is a factual statement about the analysis population.

claim: All 39 participants in the COVASE trial were followed up for 35 days or death whichever was sooner.
source: All 39 participants were followed up for 35 days or death whichever was sooner.
evidence: This is a statement about the follow-up protocol.

claim: Baseline characteristics were well balanced across groups in the COVASE trial.
source: Baseline characteristics were well balanced across groups (Table 1).
evidence: This is a statement about the comparability of study groups.

claim: The overall mean age of COVASE participants was 56.8 years.
source: The overall mean age was 56.8 years (56.8 years R-BAC +DA, 56.8 years T-BAC).
evidence: This is a demographic characteristic from the trial data.

claim: The percentage of males in the COVASE trial was 75.8%.
source: The percentage of males was 75.8% (76.7% R-BAC +DA, 75.4% T-BAC).
evidence: This is a demographic characteristic from the trial data.

claim: The mean BMI of COVASE participants was 28.0 kg/m2.
source: The mean BMI was 28.0 kg/m2 (27.8 kg/m2 R-BAC +DA, 28.2 kg/m2 T-BAC).
evidence: This is a demographic characteristic from the trial data.

claim: The mean baseline CRP post dexamethasone in the COVASE trial was 100.2 mg/L.
source: The mean baseline CRP post dexamethasone was 100.2 mg/L (101.9 mg/L R-BAC +DA, 99.5 mg/L T-BAC).
evidence: This is a baseline characteristic from the trial data.

claim: The proportion of COVASE participants with a comorbidity (hypertension, diabetes, or cardiovascular disease) was 52.5%.
source: The proportion of participants with a comorbidity, defined as one or more of hypertension, diabetes, or cardiovascular disease, was 52.5% (46.7% R-BAC +DA, 55.1% T-BAC).
evidence: This is a baseline characteristic from the trial data.

claim: All randomized COVASE participants, except one, received dexamethasone prior to randomization.
source: All randomized participants, except one, received dexamethasone prior to randomization.
evidence: This is a statement about the treatment received by participants.

claim: 48 of the total 99 COVASE participants also received remdesivir or tocilizumab in addition to dexamethasone within the first 7 days.
source: In addition, 48 of the total 99 participants also received remdesivir or tocilizumab in addition to dexamethasone within the first 7 days.
evidence: This is a statement about additional treatments received.

claim: Deceased COVID-19 participants had significantly higher plasma CRP concentrations than the participants who survived.
source: This analysis revealed that deceased participants had significantly higher plasma CRP concentrations than the participants who survived (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is a finding from the Berlin cohort analysis with reference to Figure 2A.

claim: The frequency of mortality in COVID-19 patients increased proportionally to the average CRP concentration per patient.
source: Clustering the 63 participants according to their longitudinal average CRP concentration indicated that the frequency of mortality increased proportionally to the average CRP concentration per patient (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is a finding from the Berlin cohort analysis with reference to Figure 2B.

claim: Survival in COVID-19 patients decreased significantly as the average CRP concentration increased.
source: Consistently, Mantel Cox survival analysis of the participants segregated into three groups with average longitudinal CRP concentration ranges of 0–100 mg/L, 100–200 mg/L, and 200–450 mg/L, showed that survival decreased significantly as the average CRP concentration increased (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is a finding from the Berlin cohort analysis with reference to Figure 2C.

claim: Blood CRP concentration is a strong predictor of clinical outcomes in hospitalized individuals with severe COVID-19 pneumonia.
source: These results highlighted the strong correlation between plasma CRP and the probability of survival in hospitalized individuals with severe COVID-19 pneumonia, suggesting that the blood CRP concentration was a strong predictor of clinical outcomes.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the Berlin cohort analysis results.

claim: In the randomized COVASE participants, the LS mean Ln (CRP) over 7 days follow-up was 3.10 (95% CI 2.84–3.35) in R-BAC +DA (n=30).
source: In the participants who were randomized into the COVASE trial, excluding the CC-BAC participants the LS mean Ln (CRP) over 7 days follow-up was 3.10 (95% confidence interval [CI] 2.84–3.35) in R-BAC +DA (n=30), and 3.59 (95% CI, 3.13–4.06) in R-BAC (n=9) participants (Table 2 and Figure 3A).
evidence: This is a primary outcome result from the trial data.

claim: In the randomized COVASE participants, the LS mean Ln (CRP) over 7 days follow-up was 3.59 (95% CI, 3.13–4.06) in R-BAC (n=9) participants.
source: In the participants who were randomized into the COVASE trial, excluding the CC-BAC participants the LS mean Ln (CRP) over 7 days follow-up was 3.10 (95% confidence interval [CI] 2.84–3.35) in R-BAC +DA (n=30), and 3.59 (95% CI, 3.13–4.06) in R-BAC (n=9) participants (Table 2 and Figure 3A).
evidence: This is a primary outcome result from the trial data.

claim: In the ITT group of the COVASE trial, the LS mean Ln (CRP) over 7 days follow-up was 3.15 (95% CI 2.87–3.42) in R-BAC +DA (n=30).
source: Moreover, in the ITT group which included randomized and CC-BAC groups, the LS mean Ln (CRP) over 7 days follow-up was 3.15 (95% confidence interval [CI] 2.87–3.42) in R-BAC +DA (n=30), and 3.55 (95% CI, 3.35–3.75) in T-BAC (n=69) groups (Table 2 and Figure 3A), p=0.01.
evidence: This is a primary outcome result from the trial data.

claim: In the ITT group of the COVASE trial, the LS mean Ln (CRP) over 7 days follow-up was 3.55 (95% CI, 3.35–3.75) in T-BAC (n=69) groups.
source: Moreover, in the ITT group which included randomized and CC-BAC groups, the LS mean Ln (CRP) over 7 days follow-up was 3.15 (95% confidence interval [CI] 2.87–3.42) in R-BAC +DA (n=30), and 3.55 (95% CI, 3.35–3.75) in T-BAC (n=69) groups (Table 2 and Figure 3A), p=0.01.
evidence: This is a primary outcome result from the trial data.

claim: Dornase alfa reduced mean CRP by approximately 33% in the R-BAC +DA group (23.23 mg/mL) compared to the T-BAC group (34.82 mg/mL) at mean follow-up over 7 days.
source: This indicates a reduction in mean CRP of approximately 33% in the R-BAC +DA group (23.23 mg/mL) compared to the T-BAC group (34.82 mg/mL) at mean follow-up over 7 days.
evidence: This is a calculated result from the primary outcome data.

claim: Compared to T-BAC, the R-BAC +DA treatment group exhibited a higher CRP reduction distribution with fewer participants that did not respond to anti-inflammatory therapy.
source: Compared to T-BAC, the R-BAC +DA treatment group exhibited a higher CRP reduction distribution with fewer participants that did not respond to anti-inflammatory therapy as indicated by an increase in CRP concentrations over the course of the 7 day treatment period.
evidence: This is an observation from the frequency distribution analysis.

claim: The addition of dornase alfa to dexamethasone resulted in a significant and sustained reduction in CRP in a greater number of COVID-19-infected participants compared to treatment with dexamethasone alone.
source: Therefore, the addition of dornase alfa to dexamethasone resulted in a significant and sustained reduction in CRP in a greater number of COVID-19-infected participants compared to treatment with dexamethasone alone.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the CRP analysis results.

claim: The hazard ratio for alive discharge from hospital in the COVASE trial was 1.63 (95% CI, 1.01–2.61), p=0.03.
source: The hazard ratio observed in the Cox proportional hazards model was 1.63 (95% CI, 1.01–2.61), p=0.03 (Figure 3C and Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a secondary outcome result from the trial data.

claim: Throughout the 35 day follow-up period, COVASE participants receiving dornase alfa had a 63% higher chance of discharge alive than the T-BAC control group.
source: Therefore, throughout the 35 day follow-up period, participants receiving dornase alfa had a 63% higher chance of discharge alive than the T-BAC control group.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the hazard ratio for discharge.

claim: 80% discharge occurred by 8 days in the R-BAC +DA group whereas the same proportion was reached at 30 days for T-BAC participants.
source: Although the rate of discharge was similar in 50% of participants, 80% discharge occurred by 8 days in the R-BAC +DA group whereas, whereas the same proportion was reached at 30 days for T-BAC participants.
evidence: This is an observation from the time-to-discharge analysis.

claim: Over 7 days of follow up there was no significant difference between the R-BAC +DA and T-BAC groups in the fraction of participants admitted to ICU (23.3% vs 21.74%), p=0.866.
source: Over 7 days of follow up there was no significant difference between the R-BAC +DA and T-BAC groups in either the fraction of participants admitted to ICU (23.3% vs 21.74%), p=0.866, or the length of ICU stay, LS mean 21.25 (95% CI, 4.65–37.84) hr versus 19.85 (95% CI, 8.00–31.70) hr, p=0.883.
evidence: This is a secondary outcome result from the trial data.

claim: Over 7 days of follow up there was no significant difference between the R-BAC +DA and T-BAC groups in the length of ICU stay, LS mean 21.25 (95% CI, 4.65–37.84) hr versus 19.85 (95% CI, 8.00–31.70) hr, p=0.883.
source: Over 7 days of follow up there was no significant difference between the R-BAC +DA and T-BAC groups in either the fraction of participants admitted to ICU (23.3% vs 21.74%), p=0.866, or the length of ICU stay, LS mean 21.25 (95% CI, 4.65–37.84) hr versus 19.85 (95% CI, 8.00–31.70) hr, p=0.883.
evidence: This is a secondary outcome result from the trial data.

claim: Over 35 days follow up, one person amongst the 30 patients in the R-BAC +DA group died, compared to 8 of the 69 T-BAC participants.
source: Over 35 days follow up, one person amongst the 30 patients in the R-BAC +DA group died, compared to 8 of the 69 T-BAC participants.
evidence: This is a mortality outcome from the trial data.

claim: The hazard ratio for death in the COVASE trial was 0.47 (95% CI, 0.06–3.86), p=0.460.
source: The hazard ratio observed in the Cox proportional hazards model was 0.47 (95% CI, 0.06–3.86), indicating a trend towards a reduced chance of death at any given time-point in R-BAC +DA compared to T-BAC, but this did not reach significance p=0.460 (Figure 3D and Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a mortality outcome result from the trial data.

claim: R-BAC +DA exhibited higher lymphocyte counts with an LS mean of 1.08 (95% CI, 0.92–1.27) compared to 0.87 (95% CI, 0.76–0.98) in the T-BAC group, p=0.02.
source: First, R-BAC +DA exhibited higher lymphocyte counts with an LS mean of 0.87 (95% CI, 0.76–0.98) in the T-BAC group vs. 1.08 (95% CI, 0.92–1.27) in R-BAC +DA participants, p=0.02 (Supplementary file 1B).
evidence: This is a blood analysis result from the trial data.

claim: Amongst individuals with lymphopenia at baseline, the R-BAC +DA group exhibited a greater increase in blood lymphocyte numbers compared to the T-BAC group throughout the entire length of treatment.
source: Amongst individuals with lymphopenia at baseline (<1 × 109 lymphocytes/L), the R-BAC +DA group exhibited a greater increase in blood lymphocyte numbers compared to the T-BAC group throughout the entire length of treatment (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is a subgroup analysis result from the trial data with reference to Figure 4A.

claim: D-dimer levels were lower in R-BAC +DA participants compared to T-BAC participants, with an LS mean D-dimer difference of 1657 (95% CI, 3131–877).
source: Furthermore, D-dimer levels were lower in R-BAC +DA participants compared to T-BAC participants, with an LS mean D-dimer difference of 1657 (95% CI, 3131–877) (Figure 4B, Supplementary file 1B).
evidence: This is a blood analysis result from the trial data with reference to Figure 4B.

claim: R-BAC +DA participants exhibited lower PCT concentrations, mean 0.18 ng/mL (95% CI, –0.2–0.56) compared to the T-BAC group, mean 1.31 ng/mL (95% CI, 0.56–2.05), p=0.005.
source: R-BAC +DA participants also exhibited lower PCT concentrations, mean 0.18 ng/mL (95% CI, –0.2–0.56) compared to the T-BAC group, mean 1.31 ng/mL (95% CI, 0.56–2.05), p=0.005 (Supplementary file 1B).
evidence: This is a blood analysis result from the trial data.

claim: Plasma cf-DNA levels were elevated in all R-BAC and R-BAC-DA randomized COVASE participants compared to healthy donor volunteers.
source: Compared to anonymized healthy donor volunteers at the Francis Crick institute (HD), cf-DNA levels were elevated in the plasmas of all R-BAC and R-BAC-DA randomized COVASE participants.
evidence: This is an exploratory outcome result from the trial data.

claim: There was no difference in baseline plasma cf-DNA levels between the R-BAC and R-BAC-DA randomized participant groups.
source: There was no difference in baseline plasma cf-DNA levels between the two randomized participant groups.
evidence: This is an observation from the exploratory outcome analysis.

claim: During the treatment period plasma cf-DNA was reduced in R-BAC +DA compared to R-BAC participants.
source: Notably, during the treatment period plasma cf-DNA was reduced in R-BAC +DA compared to R-BAC participants (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is an exploratory outcome result from the trial data with reference to Figure 4C.

claim: There was a positive correlation between the levels of cf-DNA in the final sample collected during the treatment period and the magnitude of CRP reduction.
source: Moreover, there was a positive correlation between the levels of cf-DNA in the final sample collected during the treatment period and the magnitude of CRP reduction measured as the ratio of the final over the baseline CRP readings (CRPfinal/CRPbaseline) (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is a correlation analysis result from the trial data with reference to Figure 4D.

claim: Plasma samples with [cf-DNA] >100 μg/mL exhibited significantly higher D-dimer levels compared to samples with [cf-DNA] <100 μg/mL.
source: Moreover, plasma samples with [cf-DNA] >100 μg/mL exhibited significantly higher D-dimer levels compared to samples with [cf-DNA] <100 μg/mL (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is a correlation analysis result from the trial data with reference to Figure 4E.

claim: Dornase alfa treatment was associated with a suppression of circulating cf-DNA that correlated with a reduced risk for coagulopathy and a more sustained reduction in CRP.
source: Hence, dornase alfa treatment was associated with a suppression of circulating cf-DNA that correlated with a reduced risk for coagulopathy and a more sustained reduction in CRP.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the exploratory outcome analyses.

claim: Dornase alfa was well tolerated with no systemic side-effects.
source: Dornase alfa was well tolerated with no systemic side-effects which is consistent with its short half-life in vivo (Supplementary file 1D).
evidence: This is a safety outcome from the trial data.

claim: There were 10 reported adverse events (AEs) in the COVASE study, in 9 R-BAC and 30 R-BAC +DA participants.
source: Overall, there were 10 reported adverse events (AEs) in the study, in 9 R-BAC and 30 R-BAC +DA participants (Supplementary file 1E).
evidence: This is a safety outcome from the trial data.

claim: One adverse event was reported by the clinical team as definitely related to dornase alfa.
source: Of these, one was reported by the clinical team as definitely related and one as unlikely to be related to dornase alfa.
evidence: This is a safety outcome from the trial data.

claim: No treatment-related serious AEs were reported in the COVASE trial.
source: No treatment-related serious AEs were reported.
evidence: This is a safety outcome from the trial data.

claim: Nebulized dornase alfa significantly reduced systemic inflammation as measured by plasma CRP concentrations in patients with severe COVID-19 pneumonia even when already receiving dexamethasone.
source: Our findings show that nebulized dornase alfa significantly reduced systemic inflammation as measured by plasma CRP concentrations in patients with severe COVID-19 pneumonia even when already receiving dexamethasone.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion from the trial findings.

claim: Dornase alfa exhibited a robust anti-inflammatory effect as assessed by several sensitivity analyses including analysis of only the randomized participant groups.
source: Dornase alfa exhibited a robust anti-inflammatory effect as assessed by several sensitivity analyses including analysis of only the randomized participant groups, by excluding CC-BAC participants.
evidence: This is a statement about the robustness of the findings.

claim: Despite not being formally powered for length of stay, dornase alfa reduced time to discharge over 35 days.
source: Moreover, despite not being formally powered for length of stay, dornase alfa reduced time to discharge over 35 days.
evidence: This is a statement about a secondary outcome finding.

claim: The finding that dornase alfa can significantly reduce CRP in participants receiving dexamethasone suggests a complementary mechanism of action with significant improvement in existing standard anti-inflammatory care.
source: The finding that dornase alfa can significantly reduce CRP in participants receiving dexamethasone suggests a complementary mechanism of action with significant improvement in existing standard anti-inflammatory care.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the trial results.

claim: Dornase alfa may be a treatment choice for patients with mild COVID-19 pneumonia not requiring oxygen, in whom dexamethasone may be harmful.
source: Moreover, dornase alfa may be a treatment choice for patients with mild COVID-19 pneumonia not requiring oxygen, in whom dexamethasone may be harmful (Galván-Román et al., 2021).
evidence: This is a speculative statement about potential applications with a citation.

claim: The reduction in hospital occupancy during the COVID-19 pandemic proved critical in sustaining life-saving treatment availability.
source: The reduction in hospital occupancy during the COVID-19 pandemic proved critical in sustaining life-saving treatment availability.
evidence: This is a statement about the broader context and importance of the findings.

claim: CRP levels are associated with venous thromboembolic disease in COVID-19 with the worst outcomes seen in patients with high CRP and D-dimer concentrations.
source: In addition to the increased mortality data we provide here, CRP levels are associated with venous thromboembolic disease in COVID-19 with the worst outcomes seen in patients with high CRP and D-dimer concentrations (Smilowitz et al., 2021).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: In a metanalysis of 32 studies involving 10,491 COVID-19 patients, lymphopenia (OR 3.33, p<0.00001), elevated CRP (OR 4.37, p<0.00001), D-dimer (OR 3.39, p<0.00001) and PCT (OR 6.33, p<0.00001) concentrations were independent markers of poor outcomes.
source: In a metanalysis of 32 studies involving 10 491 COVID-19 patients, lymphopenia (3.33, p<0.00001), elevated CRP (OR 4.37, p<0.00001), D-dimer (3.39, p<0.00001) and PCT (6.33, p<0.00001) concentrations were independent markers of poor outcomes (Malik et al., 2021).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to a meta-analysis.

claim: The CATALYST study showed that the GM-CSF-blocking antibody namilumab reduced CRP even in participants treated with dexamethasone.
source: CATALYST showed in comparably small groups (usual care, 54, namilumab, 57 and infliximab, 35) that the GM-CSF-blocking antibody namilumab reduced CRP even in participants treated with dexamethasone, whereas infliximab that targets TNF-α had no significant effect on CRP.
evidence: This is a statement about findings from another trial.

claim: Infliximab that targets TNF-α had no significant effect on CRP in the CATALYST study.
source: CATALYST showed in comparably small groups (usual care, 54, namilumab, 57 and infliximab, 35) that the GM-CSF-blocking antibody namilumab reduced CRP even in participants treated with dexamethasone, whereas infliximab that targets TNF-α had no significant effect on CRP.
evidence: This is a statement about findings from another trial.

claim: Dornase alfa exhibited comparable significance in the reduction in CRP compared to standard of care as described for namilumab at a fraction of the cost.
source: Nevertheless, dornase alfa exhibited comparable significance in the reduction in CRP compared to standard of care as described for namilumab at a fraction of the cost.
evidence: This is a comparative statement about the effectiveness and cost of dornase alfa.

claim: Endonuclease therapies may prove safer than cytokine-blocking monotherapies, as they are unlikely to increase the risk of microbial co-infection.
source: Furthermore, endonuclease therapies may prove safer than cytokine-blocking monotherapies, as they are unlikely to increase the risk of microbial co-infection associated with the neutralization of cytokines that are critical for immune defence such as IL-1β, IL-6 or GM-CSF.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the potential safety advantages of endonuclease therapies.

claim: The reduction in plasma cf-DNA levels suggests that by stripping the DNA from chromatin, dornase alfa suppresses the proinflammatory properties of histones and potentiates their degradation.
source: The reduction in plasma cf-DNA levels suggests that by stripping the DNA from chromatin, dornase alfa suppresses the proinflammatory properties of histones and potentiates their degradation (Papayannopoulos et al., 2011; Tsourouktsoglou et al., 2020).
evidence: This is an inference about the mechanism of action with citations to prior literature.

claim: The inverse correlation between the level of circulating cf-DNA and the reduction in CRP during treatment is consistent with the strong functional link between circulating chromatin and systemic inflammation observed in animal models.
source: The inverse correlation between the level of circulating cf-DNA and the reduction in CRP during treatment is consistent with the strong functional link between circulating chromatin and systemic inflammation observed in animal models (Ioannou et al., 2022).
evidence: This is an inference connecting the trial findings to prior animal model data with a citation.

claim: The correlation between D-dimer and cf-DNA provides functional validation for the suggested pro-thrombotic role of NETs in the alveoli of individuals with severe COVID-19 pneumonia.
source: Furthermore, the correlation between D-dimer and cf-DNA, as well as the reduction in D-dimer after dornase alfa treatment, provide functional validation for the suggested pro-thrombotic role of NETs in the alveoli of individuals with severe COVID-19 pneumonia (Radermecker et al., 2020).
evidence: This is an inference connecting the trial findings to a proposed mechanism with a citation.

claim: The improvement in the recovery rates of lymphopenia support the link between extracellular chromatin and lymphocyte death during sepsis in mice and humans.
source: Moreover, the improvement in the recovery rates of lymphopenia support the link between extracellular chromatin and lymphocyte death during sepsis in mice and humans that we also detected in individuals with severe COVID-19 pneumonia (Aramburu et al., 2022; Ioannou et al., 2022).
evidence: This is an inference connecting the trial findings to prior research with citations.

claim: Recombinant endonuclease treatment may be warranted in severe COVID-19 and microbial sepsis infections due to the significant reduction in endogenous NET chromatin degradation capacity that strongly correlates with a high risk for mortality.
source: Another reason why recombinant endonuclease treatment may be warranted in severe COVID-19 and microbial sepsis infections is the significant reduction in endogenous NET chromatin degradation capacity that strongly correlates with a high risk for mortality in these conditions (Aramburu et al., 2022).
evidence: This is a speculative statement about potential applications with a citation.

claim: Viral evolution and immune escape may still cause substantial mortality or symptoms associated with post-acute sequelae of SARS-CoV-2 infection (PASC), commonly known as long-COVID.
source: Whilst immunization has reduced COVID-19-related hospital admissions, viral evolution and immune escape may still cause substantial mortality or symptoms associated with post-acute sequelae of SARS-CoV-2 infection (PASC), commonly know as long-COVID.
evidence: This is a statement about ongoing challenges with COVID-19.

claim: There will always be a need for virally agnostic therapies that retain efficacy as viruses mutate.
source: Hence, there will always be a need for virally agnostic therapies that retain efficacy as viruses mutate.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about future therapeutic needs.

claim: Nebulized dornase alfa has the potential to control immune pathology in a range of infections.
source: Importantly, nebulized dornase alfa has the potential to control immune pathology in a range of infections.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about potential applications.

claim: Nebulized dornase alfa can be administered safely and effectively outside the health-care setting.
source: Moreover, it can be administered safely and effectively in its nebulized form, outside the health-care setting.
evidence: This is a statement about the practical advantages of the treatment.

claim: Three other small trials of dornase alfa (totalling 18 patients) in COVID-19 have reported improved oxygenation.
source: Three other small trials of dornase alfa (totalling 18 patients) in COVID-19 have reported improved oxygenation (Holliday et al., 2021; Okur et al., 2020; Weber et al., 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior trials.

claim: One small study indicated improvements in plasma and sputum proteomic profiles with dornase alfa treatment.
source: One small study indicated improvements in plasma and sputum proteomic profiles (Fisher et al., 2021).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to a prior study.

claim: The COVASE trial was not powered to report mortality nor to overcome confounders, such as the use of antivirals and tocilizumab.
source: However, the trial was not powered to report mortality nor to overcome confounders, such as the use of antivirals and tocilizumab, an IL-6 inhibitor recognised to reduce CRP (Galván-Román et al., 2021), or the impact of an open-label study on influencing other therapeutic/discharge decisions.
evidence: This is a statement about the limitations of the trial design.

claim: Tocilizumab is an IL-6 inhibitor recognised to reduce CRP.
source: However, the trial was not powered to report mortality nor to overcome confounders, such as the use of antivirals and tocilizumab, an IL-6 inhibitor recognised to reduce CRP (Galván-Román et al., 2021), or the impact of an open-label study on influencing other therapeutic/discharge decisions.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation.

claim: There is a trend to a reduction in CRP with dornase alfa in participants that had received tocilizumab and/or remdesivir, and those that had not.
source: Although underpowered, we demonstrate a trend to a reduction in CRP with dornase alfa in participants that had received tocilizumab and/or remdesivir, and those that had not.
evidence: This is a statement about a subgroup analysis finding.

claim: The open-label nature of the COVASE study could potentially introduce a placebo effect bias.
source: Moreover, the open-label nature of the study could potentially introduce a placebo effect bias.
evidence: This is a statement about a potential limitation of the trial design.

claim: Nebulized dornase alfa significantly reduces inflammation in hospitalised patients with severe COVID-19 pneumonia leading to improved clinical profiles and earlier discharge from hospital.
source: In conclusion, we demonstrate that nebulized dornase alfa significantly reduces inflammation in hospitalised patients with severe COVID-19 pneumonia leading to improved clinical profiles and earlier discharge from hospital.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion from the trial findings.

claim: The COVASE results confirm the role of extracellular chromatin in promoting systemic inflammation, coagulopathy and immune dysfunction in acute respiratory infections.
source: These results confirm the role of extracellular chromatin in promoting systemic inflammation, coagulopathy and immune dysfunction in acute respiratory infections and suggest that recombinant endonucleases provide an additional inexpensive mode of therapeutic intervention that can broaden the effectiveness of anti-inflammatory regimens.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the trial findings.

claim: Recombinant endonucleases provide an additional inexpensive mode of therapeutic intervention that can broaden the effectiveness of anti-inflammatory regimens.
source: These results confirm the role of extracellular chromatin in promoting systemic inflammation, coagulopathy and immune dysfunction in acute respiratory infections and suggest that recombinant endonucleases provide an additional inexpensive mode of therapeutic intervention that can broaden the effectiveness of anti-inflammatory regimens.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the trial findings.

claim: The encouraging data from the COVASE trial warrant further investigation in other serious respiratory infections characterized by hyperinflammation, cell death and NET formation.
source: These encouraging data warrant further investigation in other serious respiratory infections characterized by hyperinflammation, cell death and NET formation.
evidence: This is a recommendation for future research based on the trial findings.
